explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The Teacher says, "…one's day of death is better than his day of birth." (Ecclesiastes 7:1) Yes, he really said it, and no, I did not make my eyebrows go up on purpose. He's saying it right after the line about a good name, so I'd keep the two together.

Good guess, friend, because it sounds like something that just can't be in there. But the verse says it: "…one's day of death is better than his day of birth." (Ecclesiastes 7:1) It's a bold line, and I think the Teacher knew it would make people stop and look twice. He puts it right next to the good name, so the two go together.

That's the reason he gives, baker. The verse says, "…since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:2) So the house of mourning is a place where the living get reminded of something real. I'd rather sit there than be the guy at the feast who's too busy to notice.

I see why you'd go there, friend. Money is a classic reason to skip a party, and I've watched a lot of people stare at a bill. But the Teacher doesn't say that here. He says it's better to enter the house of mourning "…since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:2)

That's a kind thought, baker, and I like your heart. But the Teacher doesn't give that as his reason. He says, "…since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:2) His point is about what the living take from being there.

Close, but he flips it, friend. The verse says, "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure." (Ecclesiastes 7:4) So pleasure is where the fools' hearts are. The wise are over in the other house, and that's the one the Teacher wants us to notice.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, "The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure." (Ecclesiastes 7:4) The two hearts are in two different houses. He sorts them out in one short verse, and I respect a man who gets to the point.

There it is, baker. The Teacher says, "It is better to heed a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools." (Ecclesiastes 7:5) Heeding means you take it in and don't just nod. I've nodded at plenty of good advice while thinking about something else, and that's not heeding.

I get it, friend, because ignoring a rebuke is the easy move. I've done a little of it myself. But the verse says, "It is better to heed a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools." (Ecclesiastes 7:5) Ignoring isn't what he's recommending.

Ha, repeating it back is a fine habit, baker, but that's not the word here. The Teacher says, "It is better to heed a wise man's rebuke than to listen to the song of fools." (Ecclesiastes 7:5) Heed means to take it to heart, which goes a step past saying it again.

You got it, baker. The Teacher says, "For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:6) Loud, quick and gone before the pot gets warm. Then he adds, "This too is futile."

Not quite, friend. The rebuke of the wise is what the Teacher just said is worth heeding (Ecclesiastes 7:5). The crackling thorns go with something else: "…so is the laughter of the fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:6)

I see how you got there, since he's been talking about mourning. But the thorns aren't sorrow, baker. The verse says, "For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:6) It's the laughter that crackles.

Yes, baker. The Teacher says, "Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:7) Both warnings sit in one verse. Extortion and bribes, and neither one ends well for the heart.

Nope, it's in there, friend. The verse reads, "Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart." (Ecclesiastes 7:7) The bribe warning sits right beside the extortion one. It's a two-for-one verse.

That's the one, baker. The Teacher says, "The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one." (Ecclesiastes 7:8) Patient beats proud. I've waited on a batch to cool while everybody hovered, and I think patience is also what keeps the cookies from breaking.

Flip those, friend. The verse says, "…a patient spirit is better than a proud one." (Ecclesiastes 7:8) Proud is the one that loses. It's an easy pair to swap, because they sound like they're in a race.
Bold sounds good, baker, and I'd hire a bold person any day. But it's not one of the two the Teacher sets side by side. He says, "…a patient spirit is better than a proud one." (Ecclesiastes 7:8)

Right on, baker. The verse says, "Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:9) Anger settles in, like it's found a comfy chair. I'd rather not hand it a seat.
Good thinking, friend, kings do have a lot to be angry about. But the verse doesn't go there. It says, "…for anger settles in the lap of a fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:9)
I can see it, baker, because anger does feel like a stranger who shows up uninvited. But the Teacher's word is different. He says, "…for anger settles in the lap of a fool." (Ecclesiastes 7:9)

I'm with you on why you'd pick it, friend. Everybody asks it. But the Teacher says the opposite: "Do not say, 'Why were the old days better than these?' For it is unwise of you to ask about this." (Ecclesiastes 7:10) So he calls the question unwise.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, "Do not say, 'Why were the old days better than these?' For it is unwise of you to ask about this." (Ecclesiastes 7:10) He doesn't say it's wise. He says it's unwise, plain and simple.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner." (Ecclesiastes 7:12) Money covers you, and so does wisdom. But only wisdom is said to preserve life.

Makes sense, friend, since he just mentioned money. But the verse doesn't say that. It says, "…wisdom preserves the life of its owner." (Ecclesiastes 7:12) The comparison to money is there, but the thing preserved is life.

Good memory, baker, since a good name was the very first thing in this passage (Ecclesiastes 7:1). But in this verse the word is different. It says, "…wisdom preserves the life of its owner." (Ecclesiastes 7:12)

That's it, baker. The Teacher says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) It's a question with no one stepping forward. I'd keep my mustache in my pockets on this one.
I can see that guess, friend, but it's not what the verse asks. It says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) The word is straighten.
Not this time, baker. The verse says, "Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?" (Ecclesiastes 7:13) Nothing about hiding in it. The question is about straightening.
You got it, baker. The Teacher says, "In the day of prosperity, be joyful…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) Good days are for joy. I'll happily take that instruction, and I won't need it explained twice.
Saving is a sensible idea, friend, and I respect a full cookie jar. But that's not what the verse says to do. It says, "In the day of prosperity, be joyful…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14)
That sounds careful, baker, but it's not the instruction here. The Teacher says, "In the day of prosperity, be joyful…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) For the good days, the word is joyful.

Yes, baker. The verse says, "…consider this: God has made one of these along with the other…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) The two days come as a pair, prosperity and adversity. That's what the Teacher wants us to consider when the hard day shows up.

It's in there, friend. The verse says, "…in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other…" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) So the hard day and the good day are made together. That's the thing to consider.

explanations.answer: So a man cannot discover what comes after him
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, baker. The verse says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14) Nobody gets a peek at tomorrow. That's why I keep the ovens ready and leave the schedule to God.

explanations.answer: So people learn to save up for hard times
explanations.explanation: Saving up is wise advice, friend, but the verse doesn't give it as the reason. It says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14)

explanations.answer: So the proud are humbled and brought down low
explanations.explanation: That does sound like something from elsewhere in the Bible, baker, but it's not the reason here. The Teacher says God made one along with the other "…so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him." (Ecclesiastes 7:14)
